Research

Attention is scarce.
Its distribution is political.

I study how attention converges, how intense moments reorder political visibility, and how AI alters the people, systems, and messages competing for attention.

Media & collective attention

Media storms

Media storms are explosive increases in attention to a single story. My research develops computational methods to identify them across decades of news and explains why storms take different temporal forms—from explosive outbursts to slow boils and dominant plateaus.

Political voice

Who breaks through?

Periods of disrupted gatekeeping may open windows of opportunity for less-established political actors. I examine which actors gain exceptional visibility during storms, when they enter the story, and whether that visibility persists.

AI & society

Societal orientation in AI research

How does the composition of AI research teams shape engagement with ethical and societal concerns? This work maps a decade of AI scholarship to study interdisciplinarity, corporate collaboration, and whose priorities define responsible AI.

Emerging agenda

AI persuasion and synthetic participants

I am developing research on artificial sourcehood, receiver-contingent AI persuasion, and the validity of using large language models to simulate participants in social-science experiments.

Methodological approach

Theory, made measurable.

My work is defined by operationalizing amorphous theoretical concepts at scale. I use natural language processing, time-series analysis, experiments, and human-in-the-loop research designs to test and refine communication theory.
